question: Compare U.S. comparable sales growth (ex-fuel where reported) for Walmart U.S. (Q2 FY2027), Costco U.S. (Q4 FY2026), and Target (Q2 2026), and explain why the periods aren't directly comparable.
grading: Key points: (1) each comp figure exact as disclosed with its adjustment basis stated; (2) states each period's end date and length (16 weeks for COST); (3) explains the misalignment and definitional differences; (4) no ranking conclusion that ignores the mismatch
answer: Walmart U.S. Q2 FY2027 comp sales grew 2.6% excluding fuel, for 13 weeks ended July 31, 2026. [G30-E1] Costco U.S. Q4 FY2026 comps grew 7.2% excluding gasoline-price and FX effects, for 16 weeks ended August 30, 2026 (headline U.S. comp growth was 10.7%). [G30-E2] Target Q2 2026 comparable sales grew 3.8% for 13 weeks ended August 1, 2026, under Target’s own store-and-digital definition; the release does not present a matching gas/FX-adjusted figure. [G30-E3] The quarters differ in length, end dates and adjustment definitions: Costco’s period is three weeks longer and includes more August trading. These figures therefore do not support a directly comparable market-share ranking.

output.answer:
## Bottom line

| Retailer | Period | Reported U.S. comps | "Ex-fuel"/adjusted U.S. comps | Key one-off distorters |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Walmart U.S.** | Q2 FY2027 (13 wks, ended ~Jul 31, 2026) | **+2.6%** (ex-fuel) | **+3.4%** ex–Health & Wellness | ~**−125 bps** from pharmacy deflation under "Maximum Fair Price" regulation; tariff refunds boosted profit, not comps |
| **Costco U.S.** | Q4 FY2026 (**16 wks**, ended Aug 30, 2026) | **+10.7%** | **+7.2%** excluding gas-price inflation and FX | Gas inflation added ~**+3%** to reported comps; FX −~0.3% (global); tariff refunds helped EPS |
| **Target** | Q2 2026 (13 wks, ended Aug 1, 2026) | **+3.8%** | Same (Target reports one comp figure) | Store comps +2.7%, digital +8.7%; tariff refunds boosted EPS, not comps |

Sources: [Walmart Q2 FY27 release](https://corporate.walmart.com/news/2026/08/20/walmart-releases-q2-fy27-earnings), [Walmart earnings release PDF](https://stock.walmart.com/_assets/_8c8425b76a1d46bbbbc16466da2a6b9c/walmart/db/938/9996/earnings_release/Earnings+Release+%28FY27+Q2%29.pdf), [Costco Q4 FY26 results](https://investor.costco.com/news/news-details/2026/Costco-Wholesale-Corporation-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2026-Operating-Results/default.aspx), [Costco IR PDF](https://s201.q4cdn.com/287523651/files/doc_news/Costco-Wholesale-Corporation-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2026-Operating-Results-2026.pdf), [Target Q2 2026 release](https://corporate.target.com/press/release/2026/08/target-corporation-reports-second-quarter-earnings), [CNBC on Target](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/19/target-tgt-q2-2026-earnings.html).

## Why they aren't directly comparable

**1. Fiscal calendars don't align (and periods differ in length).**
- Walmart's fiscal year ends Jan 31; Q2 FY27 = roughly **May 1 – Jul 31, 2026 (13 weeks)**.
- Target's fiscal year also ends late Jan/early Feb; Q2 2026 = **May 3 – Aug 1, 2026 (13 weeks)**.
- Costco's fiscal year ends in late August, and it reports **12-12-12-16-week** quarters, so Q4 FY26 = **16 weeks ended Aug 30, 2026**.

So Costco's quarter is **~23% longer** and runs nearly a month later — capturing more of the back-to-school season and late-summer traffic that Walmart's and Target's quarters largely miss. Even where the windows overlap, you're comparing different amounts of calendar.

**2. Different comp definitions.**
- **Walmart** reports U.S. comps **excluding fuel** (fuel is a separate, excluded line) and includes eCommerce and remodeled/relocated stores in the base. It also offers a supplemental "ex–Health & Wellness" figure of **+3.4%** to strip out pharmacy volatility.
- **Costco**'s headline comp **includes gasoline**; its "adjusted" number strips out both **gas-price inflation and FX**. Headline (10.7%) vs. adjusted (7.2%) is a ~350 bps gap driven almost entirely by gas.
- **Target** reports a single comp figure (store + digital combined); unlike Costco, it has no fuel business, and unlike Walmart, no separate "ex-pharmacy" adjustment.

Comparing Walmart's "ex-fuel" number to Costco's **including-gas** headline (10.7%) would be apples-to-oranges; the fair Costco line is the **7.2% adjusted** figure.

**3. Business mix differs fundamentally.**
- **Costco** is a membership warehouse club: food/consumables dominate, groceries are often ~60% of sales, and it benefits from traffic-led, value-seeking behavior (traffic +3.3% worldwide in Q4). Its comps are structurally more food-driven and less discretionary.
- **Walmart U.S.** is a mass merchant with roughly 60% grocery but a large general-merchandise and health & wellness component — the latter being the source of its 125 bps pharmacy drag this quarter.
- **Target** is the most discretionary-heavy (~20–25% food), so its comp reflects apparel/home cycles. Its +3.8% was driven by traffic (+3.6%) with flat ticket, aided by digital/same-day delivery growth — a very different driver set than Costco's ticket-led growth or Walmart's transaction-led growth.

**4. Different one-time distorters in the period.**
- Walmart: **−125 bps** from pharmacy deflation/brand-to-generic transfers under the new Maximum Fair Price regulation (company said underlying core categories were steady with prior trends).
- Costco: **~+3%** tailwind from gas-price inflation in the reported figure.
- Target and Walmart/Costco all booked **IEEPA tariff refunds**, but those flowed to **gross margin/EPS, not comps**, so they inflate earnings comparisons without affecting the sales-growth lines being compared.

**Net effect:** on a somewhat normalized basis, Costco U.S. (7.2% adjusted) is growing comps far faster than Walmart U.S. (~3.4% ex-H&W) and Target (3.8%) — but that gap is partly a function of Costco's longer, later quarter, its food-heavy mix, and gas inflation, not a pure like-for-like read on underlying demand.
